extracted.intended_audience: Citizens and voters (specifically the People of the State of New York) evaluating the proposed U.S. Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and argumentative standards for assessing the constitutional design and powers of the United States Senate (treaty-making, appointments, impeachment jurisdiction, term lengths, representation, secrecy, and checks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of appointment (select electors / state legislatures)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President to be chosen by select bodies of electors; the appointment of senators committed to the State legislatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: Appointments by select assemblies or legislatures have the advantage over direct popular elections because such bodies will generally be composed of the most enlightened and respectable citizens and thus are more likely to choose men 'distinguished by their abilities and virtue.' This mode reduces the influence of transient party zeal and the votes of an uninformed or easily-deceived mass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age qualifications for officeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: By excluding men under thirty-five from the first office, and those under thirty from the second, the Constitution confines electors to men of whom the people have had time to form a judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: age thresholds help ensure electors have had opportunity to judge character and reduce susceptibility to being deceived by 'brilliant appearances' of genius or patriotism; thus improve the quality and reliability of appointments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration and continuity of Senate service (staggered six-year terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: The duration prescribed is such as will give them an opportunity of greatly extending their political information, and of rendering their accumulating experience more and more beneficial to their country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: Longer, staggered terms provide continuity and allow senators to acquire exact information and craft steady systems for long-term national affairs (trade, navigation, treaties). Frequent rotation of all members would be inadequate for such sustained business; leaving a residue of experienced members preserves uniformity, order, and official memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secrecy and immediate despatch in treaty negotiation
rubrics_metrics.description: It seldom happens in the negotiation of treaties ... but that perfect secrecy and immediate despatch are sometimes requisite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: Treaty-making requires occasions where secrecy and prompt action are essential to obtain useful intelligence and to act on transient diplomatic opportunities. The constitutional arrangement (President + Senate advice/consent) balances deliberation and secrecy by permitting the President to manage intelligence and call the Senate when consent is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-thirds Senate concurrence for treaties
rubrics_metrics.description: The second section gives power to the President, 'BY AND WITH THE ADVICE AND CONSENT OF THE SENATE, TO MAKE TREATIES, PROVIDED TWO THIRDS OF THE SENATORS PRESENT CONCUR.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Function: The supermajority requirement is presented as a safeguard to ensure treaties are formed by well-qualified men and have wide support in the Senate; combined with the appointment method and Senate composition it increases confidence that treaties will serve the public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaties as binding and supreme law (not repealable at pleasure)
rubrics_metrics.description: They insist that treaties like acts of assembly, should be repealable at pleasure. ... A treaty is only another name for a bargain ... as the consent of both was essential to their formation at first, so must it ever afterwards be to alter or cancel them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: Treaties bind both parties; allowing unilateral repealability would ruin international bargains. Therefore treaties should remain supreme and not be trivially revocable by one party alone; changing them also requires mutual consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: State equality in Senate representation protects state interests
rubrics_metrics.description: As all the States are equally represented in the Senate, and by men the most able and the most willing to promote the interests of their constituents, they will all have an equal degree of influence in that body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical note: Equal state representation in the Senate gives each State influence in treaty and appointment matters, mitigating fears that some States will be consistently oppressed; proper appointments and punctual attendance by State legislatures are important to realize this protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of risk of senatorial aristocracy via corruption pathway
rubrics_metrics.description: Before such a revolution can be effected, the Senate ... must in the first place corrupt itself; must next corrupt the State legislatures; must then corrupt the House of Representatives; and must finally corrupt the people at large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic criterion: To judge whether a Senate will become an aristocracy, consider the plausibility of the sequential corruption of multiple institutions and the people. The chain of required corruptions makes such a revolution improbable; experience (e.g., Maryland, Britain, ancient examples) supports this view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate as fit tribunal for impeachment (dignity, independence, numerosity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where else than in the Senate could have been found a tribunal sufficiently dignified, or sufficiently independent? ... The necessity of a numerous court for the trial of impeachments, is equally dictated by the nature of the proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: Impeachments are political, passion-inflaming, and require a body capable of impartiality and public confidence; the Senate's dignity, independence, and sufficient size make it better suited than small permanent courts or the Supreme Court; a numerous body reduces risk of partisan persecution and safeguards fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court unsuitable as sole impeachment court
rubrics_metrics.description: It is much to be doubted, whether the members of that tribunal would at all times be endowed with so eminent a portion of fortitude ... and it is still more to be doubted, whether they would possess the degree of credit and authority ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concerns: The Supreme Court might lack the public authority to reconcile people to decisions against accusations by representatives; combining impeachment judgment with later criminal trials by the same judges risks biasing subsequent proceedings and undermines double security intended by separate trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid combining impeachment judgment with later criminal adjudication by same actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Would it be proper that the persons who had disposed of his fame ... should, in another trial, for the same offense, be also the disposers of his life and his fortune? ... error, in the first sentence, would be the parent of error in the second sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle: Structural separation (different bodies for political impeachment and criminal prosecution) protects accused persons from compounded error and bias; using the same judges in both proceedings risks prejudicing subsequent trials and undermining fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial intermixture of powers permissible for special purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: The true meaning of this maxim ... has been shown to be entirely compatible with a partial intermixture of those departments for special purposes, preserving them, in the main, distinct and unconnected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: The doctrine of separation of powers allows limited cross-department roles (e.g., legislative body acting as impeachment court) when necessary as checks and balances; absolute separation is neither required nor practical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical feasibility and costs of alternative impeachment tribunals
rubrics_metrics.description: A court formed upon such a plan, would either be attended with a heavy expense, or might in practice be subject to a variety of casualties and inconveniences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation metric: When proposing alternatives (a separate permanent court or ad hoc state officers), weigh material costs, logistical difficulty of assembling dispersed officers, delay harms to the accused and to the State, and risks of corruption or procrastination—practical concerns can justify the Senate-based solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-thirds concurrence as additional security for innocence in impeachments
rubrics_metrics.description: As the concurrence of two thirds of the Senate will be requisite to a condemnation, the security to innocence, from this additional circumstance, will be as complete as itself can desire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Function: A supermajority threshold for conviction helps protect against partisan or factional condemnations and increases confidence that impeachment convictions reflect broad agreement rather than temporary factional passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ultimate corrective: popular branch and people as check on Senate power
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides the conclusive evidence ... we are warranted in believing, that if such a revolution should ever happen ... the House of Representatives, with the people on their side, will at all times be able to bring back the Constitution to its primitive form and principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional safeguard: The popular House and ultimately the people serve as counterweights to senatorial overreach; when judging concentration of power, consider the ability of the immediate representatives of the people to restore constitutional balance.
